source.filename: A Review of Mechanisms to Vary the Stiffness of Laminar Jamming Structures and Their Applications in Robotics.pdf

actuation: electric power / thermal conditions (shape memory alloy wires)
electric power / high-voltage source (electrostatic force / electro-bonded lamination)
mechanical / pressure clamps (bolts, rubber bands, piezoelectric actuators)
heat source / thermal conditions / temperature controller (electric heating blankets)
linear actuator / solenoid / linear motorized stage (sliding-layer laminates)
air pressure / pneumatic cylinder (trapezoidal pin mechanism)
positive pressure pneumatic actuators (pneu-net actuators, McKibben artificial muscles, air bladders)
constitutive_assumptions: Inter-layer frictional behavior governed by Coulomb friction where shear resistance depends on normal force and inter-layer coefficient of friction
Beam bending behavior governed by multi-layer beam theory where uncoupled layers slide freely with low bending stiffness and fully locked layers behave as a unified cross-section
Theoretical stiffness ratio scales with the number of layers raised to the second power (N^2)
Stiffness in the pre-slip regime scales with N^3 while stiffness in the full-slip regime scales linearly with N and with the square of the friction coefficient (mu^2) and pressure (P)
Deformation energy transforms between external work, elastic bending strain energy, and inter-layer frictional dissipation
control_variables: Specimen dimensions including layer length, width, thickness, and slenderness ratio
Layer materials (e.g., Mylar films, polyimide, aluminum, spring steel, paper, sandpaper, silicone)
Operating ambient pressure and room temperature during testing
Electrical current limits (e.g., limiting current to 1 mA in electrostatic gloves for human safety)
Mechanical clamp spacing and number of guide frames preventing layer buckling without applying normal force
Displacement rate or loading speed during quasi-static bending tests
dependent_variables: Stiffness variation (stiffness ratio, defined as maximum stiffness divided by minimum stiffness)
Stiffness range (minimum to maximum stiffness values in N/mm)
Transition force threshold between pre-slip and full-slip regimes
Yield force and load-carrying capacity under external load
Deflection and angular displacement under applied mechanical force
Impact force attenuation and acceleration decay rate during collisions

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Laminar jamming modulates bending stiffness by locking or unlocking thin sheets, transitioning between an uncoupled flexible state where layers slide and a locked rigid state where layers bend as a unified structure.
The theoretical stiffness ratio of laminar jamming structures is proportional to the number of layers squared, though physical friction and lock/unlock mechanism efficacy constrain real-world values.
SMA-wrapped laminar jamming structures achieved a stiffness variation of 60x with a stiffness range of 0.03 to 1.8 N/mm, but are limited by slow heating and cooling times of 100 s and 200 s.

Electrostatic layer jamming mechanisms utilize alternating polarity high-voltage polyimide layers to achieve up to 18x stiffness variation with fast response times under 5 ms actuation and 15 ms release.
Vacuum-pressure-activated laminar jamming is the most prevalent friction-based method, offering stiffness variations between 10x and 180x and a stiffness range from 0.008 to 1.522 N/mm.

Discrete laminar jamming (DLJ) utilizes discrete variable pressure clamps (bolts, rubber bands, or piezoelectric actuators) eliminating the elastic membrane and vacuum sealing issues, demonstrating a 17x stiffness variation.
Mechanical interference mechanisms use actuators (such as SMA or electroactive polymers) to engage teeth into gaps between layers, yielding up to 14.6x stiffness variation.
Laminar jamming structures using heating blankets achieve low stiffness variation (2.25x to 4x) across a high stiffness range of approximately 5 to 18 N/mm, with slow thermal switching speeds.
Sliding-layer laminates (SLL) alternate rigid and soft segments to adjust stiffness by 3x to 7x over a 0.005 to 0.035 N/mm range using linear actuators with ~4 s transition times.

Laminar jamming combined with positive pressure pneumatic actuators (e.g. pneu-nets or McKibben artificial muscles) enables decoupled control of bending shape and structural stiffness in soft robotic grippers and fingers.

Continuum robots employ tubular configurations of overlapping multi-flap Mylar films or mesh sheaths with internal backbone springs to vary bending stiffness for minimally invasive surgery and bioinspired structures.

Wearable robotic applications include soft layer jamming linear brakes (SLJB) and sliding linkage mechanisms providing variable stiffness and braking in axial tension and bending for spinal, elbow, wrist, and finger rehabilitation.

In robot arms, dual parallel-guided beam links containing solid compliant backbones flanked by vacuum laminar jamming jammers improve vertical and torsional stability while providing compliance for impact mitigation.
The trapezoidal pin mechanism combines discrete mechanical clamping with mechanical interference via a pneumatic cylinder to provide variable stiffness while guide frames prevent layer buckling.

Vacuum-activated laminar jamming exhibits a switching time constant of approximately 0.5 s, which is too slow to mitigate active collisions with humans where impact damage occurs in approximately 0.1 s.
Under excessive external loading, vacuum laminar jamming transitions from pre-slip to full-slip regime, dropping stiffness and risking catastrophic yielding if load is maintained.
Finite element analysis (FEA) has demonstrated high fidelity for laminar jamming mechanics with coefficients of determination (R^2) reaching 0.9879 against experimental data.
Recent analytical formulations for arbitrary numbers of layers offer computationally efficient alternatives to FEA where simulation runtime increases substantially with layer count.

experimental_setup: Cantilever quasi-static bending tests measuring force versus deflection curves for multi-layer laminar beams
Three-point and four-point bending test benches evaluating flexural rigidity across various actuation states
Axial tensile force loading test rigs for soft layer jamming linear brakes (SLJB)
High-voltage electric excitation circuits with alternating electrode polarity for electrostatic layer jamming tests
Regulated vacuum pump systems with pressure sensors and manual flexure protocols for envelope depressurization
Thermal cycling rigs with thermocouple monitoring for SMA-wrapped and heating-blanket jamming structures
Dynamic impact collision rigs measuring force and acceleration profiles between variable stiffness robotic arm links and impactors
Underwater swimming testing tanks using stepper motors and linear solenoids to drive flapping motion in SLL robot fish tails
Multi-DoF robotic wrist testbeds evaluating bidirectional orthogonal stiffness modulation and dynamic damping
future_work: Quantitatively measuring and reporting stiffening and destiffening velocities across all lock/unlock mechanisms
Developing fast lock/unlock mechanisms, such as discrete laminar jamming with piezoelectric actuators, to enable active collision mitigation
Combining fundamental laminar jamming mechanisms, such as vacuum pressure with mechanical interference, to boost stiffness ratio and maintain compactness
Implementing electrostatic layer jamming in robotic arm links to exploit millisecond-scale actuation (<5 ms) and release (<15 ms) speeds
Hybridizing laminar jamming with other variable stiffness methods such as shape-morphing air bladders and pneumatic chambers
Developing closed-loop control algorithms for variable stiffness links and joints to regulate impedance, directional stiffness, and impact attenuation
Extending design methodologies and computational design frameworks beyond vacuum-actuated jamming to other laminar jamming mechanisms
Improving reporting of manufacturing techniques, material wear, failure modes, and long-term repeatability degradation
independent_variables: Number of layers in the stack (N)
Vacuum / negative pressure level applied to the chamber (P)
Magnitude of applied voltage / electric field (for electrostatic jamming)
Applied electric current / thermal energy (for SMA and heating blanket mechanisms)
Number, shape, and insertion depth/location of teeth or pins (for mechanical interference and trapezoidal pin mechanisms)
Clamping pressure set by discrete bolts, rubber bands, or actuators (for DLJ)
Relative sliding displacement and overlap fraction of rigid versus soft segments (for sliding-layer laminates)
Geometric dimensions of the beam including length, width, layer thickness, and slenderness ratio
limitations_inferred: Because data are synthesized from heterogeneous research papers with differing beam geometries, materials, and test setups, direct numerical comparison across mechanisms is subject to confounding factors.
Replacing vacuum envelopes with discrete mechanical clamps or piezoelectric actuators may introduce parasitic mass, rigidity, and wiring complexity that could compromise soft robotic advantages.
Long-term cyclic fatigue, permanent layer deformation, and friction surface degradation under millions of cycles remain uncharacterized in dynamic operations.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Vacuum-pressure laminar jamming switching speeds (~0.5 s time constant) are too slow for active impact mitigation during collisions (~0.1 s duration).
Vacuum laminar jamming drops in stiffness when transitioning from pre-slip to full-slip regimes, which can cause catastrophic yielding under maintained high loads.
Vacuum envelopes present sealing challenges, susceptibility to damage or puncture from rough edges, and incomplete release requiring manual flexing.
SMA-wrapped mechanisms exhibit long thermal switching cycles (100 s heating, 200 s cooling), wire relaxation after thermal cycling, and manual assembly inconsistencies.
Electrostatic jamming historically required dangerously high voltages (hundreds to thousands of volts) for human interaction.
Most tested laminar jamming structures are limited in length (<= 400 mm) and cannot immediately scale to industrial-sized robotic arms.
Materials such as paper and sandpaper experience rapid surface wear, reducing repeatability and durability over repeated bending cycles.
Existing systematic design methodologies and automated design scripts are restricted exclusively to vacuum-pressure jamming.
Published literature frequently lacks detailed manufacturing documentation, design iteration rationale, and degradation data over time.
main_results: Friction-based mechanisms provide the highest stiffness variations among all mechanisms, reaching up to 180x for vacuum pressure and 60x for SMA wrapping.

Vacuum-pressure laminar jamming is the most versatile and developed mechanism, exhibiting the widest stiffness range (0.008 to 1.522 N/mm) and suitability across grippers, continuum robots, wearable devices, and robot arms.
Thermal-activated mechanisms (SMA and heating blankets) have the lowest switching speeds (100 s to 200 s), making them unsuitable for active dynamic impact mitigation.

Current vacuum-activated laminar jamming structures have reaction time constants around 0.5 s, which exceeds the ~0.1 s impact damage threshold, limiting them primarily to passive compliance applications.
Electrostatic jamming can achieve ultra-fast switching (<5 ms actuation, <15 ms release) while current-limiting circuits (1 mA) mitigate electrical hazards in wearable applications.

Finite element analysis accurately predicts laminar jamming behavior (R^2 up to 0.9879), and modern analytical models provide efficient modeling for arbitrary layer counts without excessive computation.
modeling_methods: Energy method (conservation of external work, elastic bending strain energy, and inter-layer frictional work)
Analytical beam models for arbitrary numbers of layers
Pseudo-rigid-body modeling (for parallel guided beam compliant links)
Model-based design frameworks and computational design scripts (e.g. Matlab-based design tools)
performance_metrics: Stiffness variation (stiffness ratio, maximum stiffness / minimum stiffness)
Speed of stiffening (actuation time, ms or s)
Speed of destiffening (release/destiffening time, ms or s)
Yield force threshold / pre-slip to full-slip transition force (N)
Torsional stiffness and critical vertical buckling load
Pinch grasp force and grasp stability for various object sizes
Impact peak force reduction and acceleration attenuation during collision
Coefficient of determination (R^2) between model and experimental data
possible_gap_implications: Identifying that vacuum laminar jamming switching speeds (~0.5 s) exceed collision timescales (~0.1 s) highlights a clear research gap for fast-response locking mechanisms in active safe cobots, though developing faster mechanisms requires solving actuation weight and force density trade-offs.

The absence of standardized metrics for stiffening/destiffening speeds and endurance/wear testing across the literature represents a methodological gap that, if addressed, could enable objective cross-comparison and industrial adoption.
paper.research_objective: To review the lock/unlock mechanisms of laminar jamming structures, examine their robotic applications (including grippers, continuum robots, wearable robots, and robot arms), analyze their performance and limitations with an emphasis on human-robot impact mitigation, evaluate analytical and finite element modeling methods, and provide future research directions.
paper.research_problem: Robotic systems require variable stiffness links and joints to combine the payload capacity and precision of rigid robots with the safety and adaptability of soft robots; however, existing laminar jamming lock/unlock mechanisms face performance trade-offs in stiffening/destiffening speed, stiffness range, envelope durability, and scalability, particularly for mitigating collisions in human-robot interaction.
paper.robot_type: soft grippers and fingers, continuum robots, wearable robots (exoskeletons, haptic gloves, and soft linear brakes), robot arms (variable stiffness links and joints), unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) landing gear, and underwater robots (robot fish)
stiffness_mechanism: laminar jamming wrapped by shape memory alloy (SMA)
electrostatic force / electrostatic layer jamming / electro-bonded lamination
mechanical interference (teeth-clutching / form closure / smart form closure actuators)
trapezoidal pin mechanism (discrete laminar jamming combined with mechanical interference)
vacuum pressure combined with mechanical interference (multi-material teeth-clutching layer jamming)
hybrid jamming (laminar jamming combined with particle jamming)
hybrid variable stiffness link (airtight chamber, shape morphing, and laminar jamming)
paper.title: A Review of Mechanisms to Vary the Stiffness of Laminar Jamming Structures and Their Applications in Robotics
